extracted.intended_audience: general public, educators, policymakers, and workers interested in education reform
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the harms and benefits of centralized/state-run education versus voluntary/local education, focusing on moral, social, administrative, and pedagogical effects. The page argues criteria by which to judge whether state education is a help or hindrance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on family moral development
rubrics_metrics.description: Intruding a huge, all-powerful something you call the state between parents and children undermines affection, sympathy, and restraint of the graspings of self for the good of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The state telling parents 'You need trouble yourself no more about the education of your children' removes opportunities for parents to acquire patience and unselfishness; treating people as unworthy of trust produces passive acceptance of the mental and moral condition created for them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding mechanism fairness and class interference
rubrics_metrics.description: Forced payments taken from other classes place the workman under an obligation and cause upper and middle classes to interfere in the education of his children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compulsory taxation/grants tied to state education create political obligations and open the system to manipulation by classes with greater influence; this politicizes education and reduces the agency of working-class families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pluralism and freedom for personal views
rubrics_metrics.description: Under a political system there is no place for personal views; one body acting for a whole country can only pursue one method and therefore excludes views not in accordance with that method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralized systems favor a single official method, forcing individuals to join existing parties or accept majority-determined policies rather than pursue alternative educational philosophies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity and experimental freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformity in education is injurious; progress is difference (Herbert Spencer). If you desire progress, you must not make it difficult for men to think and act differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A national uniform system (same teachers, inspectors, examinations, and standards) blocks innovators: reformers need immediate opportunities to try experiments and to collect funds and supporters; national uniformity makes small-scale experimentation nearly impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspections and standards bias against innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Inspectors' eyes are trained to see perfection of only one kind, and they may summarily condemn an experimental school as 'inefficient' and disallow it by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Central inspection regimes tend to enforce conformity and penalize schools that apply new methods; reliance on inspectors as gatekeepers discourages experimental, tentative application of new ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative opacity and escape from control
rubrics_metrics.description: A great office which is attacked envelops itself in a cloud of technical statements which successfully confuses the public until its attention is drawn off; departments escape control and mismanagement surfaces only spasmodically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large departments accumulate technical knowledge that makes public criticism difficult; this leads to periods of unobserved mismanagement followed by spasmodic outbursts of indignation that fail to produce lasting reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsiveness to innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: A great department must be by the law of its own condition unfavorable to new ideas; to make a change it must make a revolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because central departments must issue uniform edicts without exceptions, they are structurally unfit to adopt tentative, local, or experimental changes; even energetic leadership at the center produces only spasmodic, unsustainable change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment-by-results versus broader educational aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Payment by results is simple and easy to administer but necessarily restricts and vulgarizes our conceptions of education, reducing everyone to the aim of satisfying certain regulations and passing standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems that tie public money to measurable outcomes focus teachers, pupils, and managers on standards/examinations rather than slow-bearing aims like imagination, reasoning, interest in work for its own sake, and personal influences of vocationally-chosen teachers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examinations' effect on teacher originality and personality
rubrics_metrics.description: The exaggerated use of examinations makes it impossible for teachers to treat subjects from that point of view which is real and living to themselves; they must recast and remodel themselves into humble copies of the inspector or examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuous examination regimes train teachers to reproduce what they were drilled in, destroy originality, and subordinate higher aims of teaching; inspectors' short visits cannot capture slow educational outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for conscience and religious pluralism
rubrics_metrics.description: The same arguments that condemn a national religion also condemn a national system of education: both compel some to support a system to which they are opposed and exalt the principle of majorities over individual conscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A national system risks becoming an 'established Church' of education, drawing religious minorities into supporting a system inconsistent with their principles and using it for political advantage, thereby narrowing their minds and reducing principled adherence in politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of educational content and sectarian choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Secular education, even if just, is a miserable expedient; healthier is for each section in the nation to regain perfect freedom and present life as each sees and feels it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing separate teaching by different religious or philosophical communities preserves intensity of conviction and pluralism even if it risks some narrowness, which the author prefers to the 'moral and intellectual sleepiness' of official uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of voluntary/local initiative vs government provision
rubrics_metrics.description: Government effort and individual (voluntary) effort cannot live side by side; government assistance early in the movement arrested natural voluntary growth of education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The combining and cooperative power of people (religious and social groups) could provide education; money is available from private donors if outlets are left open; government grants can blunt voluntary energy and create dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of compulsion/coercion in education
rubrics_metrics.description: Get rid of compulsion: it has been made the instrument of endless petty persecutions and is fatal to the free growth of an intelligent love of education and to true respect of man for man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compulsion cuts off home duties and labors, substitutes short cuts to progress, and copies continental paternal systems that undermine liberty; removing compulsion is presented as the first practical step for opponents of state education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local control, voluntary rates, and experimental governance
rubrics_metrics.description: Refuse the grant that the central department offers as a bribe; until self-reliance grows, let each town administer education in its own way; perhaps allow a minority of electors to choose and pay for their own board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decentralized, voluntary, and elective arrangements promote local life, energy, and variety; the suggested intermediate reform is powers enabling a fraction of electors (one sixth to one tenth) to elect a board and pay their own rates, as a step toward purely voluntary rates and full freedom of action.
